title: Real Estate Wholesaling Business Plan Step by Step: Build a Profitable Operation from Scratch
excerpt: A solid real estate wholesaling business plan is the difference between closing one lucky deal and building a consistent income stream. Follow this step-by-step guide to set up your wholesaling operation the right way.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: real estate wholesaling business plan step by step
metaDescription: Learn how to build a real estate wholesaling business plan step by step. Includes goals, marketing, deal flow, and scaling tips for new and experienced investors.
metaKeywords: real estate wholesaling business plan step by step, wholesaling real estate for beginners, how to start wholesaling, wholesale deal strategy, real estate investor business plan, wholesale marketing plan, build a wholesaling business

sections.content: Most people who try wholesaling quit within six months. Not because the business model is broken, but because they skipped the planning phase. A real estate wholesaling business plan step by step gives you a roadmap so you know exactly what to do on day one, day thirty, and day three hundred. Whether you're brand new or you've closed a handful of deals and want to scale, this guide covers every layer of a functioning wholesale operation. For a broader view of growing your investing business over time, check out the [Scaling a Real Estate Investing Business: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/scaling-real-estate-investing-business) before diving in.
Step 1: Define Your Business Goals and Financial Targets

Start with hard numbers, not vague dreams. Ask yourself: How much do I want to earn in the next 12 months? How many hours per week can I dedicate to this? What markets will I focus on? A realistic goal for a part-time wholesaler in their first year is $40,000 to $80,000 in assignment fees. A full-time operator targeting a hot market like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) or [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) can realistically target $150,000 to $300,000 or more once systems are in place.

items: Set a monthly revenue target (e.g., $8,000/month = ~2 deals at $4,000 avg assignment fee)
Decide on your market radius — start with one city or county before expanding
Define your preferred property type: single-family, small multifamily, or both
Establish your minimum acceptable assignment fee ($5,000 is a common floor)
Set a timeline for your first deal: most wholesalers close deal one within 60 to 90 days

sections.content: Step 2: Learn the Legal and Structural Basics

Wholesaling is legal in every state, but the rules vary. In some states, marketing a property you don't own can require a real estate license. The safest legal structure is to use an assignable purchase contract, meaning you sign a contract with the seller and then assign your equitable interest to a buyer for a fee. Form an LLC before you close your first deal. It costs $50 to $500 depending on your state and gives you liability protection. Open a separate business checking account immediately — mixing personal and business money creates accounting headaches and red flags with lenders down the road. If you're still learning the fundamentals, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide is a solid starting point.

Pro Tip: Use a transactional or double-close when selling to buyers who don't want the assignment fee visible on the HUD. A title company familiar with wholesaling can walk you through this. Ask your title company upfront if they work with wholesalers — not all of them do.
Step 3: Build Your Marketing Machine to Find Motivated Sellers

No leads, no deals. Your marketing plan is the engine of the whole operation. New wholesalers often spread themselves too thin trying every channel at once. Instead, pick two or three strategies, master them, and then layer in more. The most consistent lead sources for wholesalers are direct mail, driving for dollars, cold calling, and PPC (pay-per-click) ads. Direct mail to pre-foreclosure, probate, and tax-delinquent lists typically costs $0.60 to $1.50 per piece and generates a 1% to 3% response rate. If you mail 1,000 pieces and get 15 calls, you might turn two or three of those into motivated seller conversations.

items: Direct mail: target distressed lists like pre-foreclosures, probate, and absentee owners
Cold calling: use skip-tracing services to get phone numbers from list data
Driving for dollars: document vacant and distressed properties in your target zip codes
PPC ads: Google and Facebook campaigns targeting 'sell my house fast' keywords
Bandit signs: low-cost but effective in suburban and rural markets
Networking: REIA meetings, real estate meetups, and agent relationships

sections.content: Step 4: Master Your Numbers Before You Make Offers

The most expensive mistake a new wholesaler makes is locking up a deal at the wrong price. Your offer must account for the After Repair Value (ARV), the estimated repair cost, your buyer's profit margin, holding costs, and your assignment fee. The standard formula is: Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO) = ARV × 70% minus repair costs minus your fee. For example, if a home has an ARV of $200,000 and needs $30,000 in repairs, your MAO is $200,000 × 0.70 = $140,000 minus $30,000 minus $10,000 (your fee) = $100,000. Use the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run these numbers quickly on every deal before you make an offer.
"You make your money when you buy, not when you sell. A wholesaler who overpays for a contract has nothing to sell — they have a liability." — Common wisdom among experienced wholesale investors
Step 5: Build and Maintain Your Buyer's List

Your buyer's list is your distribution network. A deal with no buyer is worthless. Start building your list before you have a single contract. Attend local REIAs, post in Facebook wholesaling groups, and connect with cash buyers through public records (look for recent cash sales in your target zip codes). In active markets like [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), you can find dozens of active cash buyers in a single afternoon of public records research. Aim for 50 to 100 verified buyers before you go heavy on marketing — buyers who have actually closed in the last 12 months, not just people who said they buy houses.
Step 6: Set Up Your Deal Pipeline and Operations

Once leads start coming in, you need a system to track every deal from first contact to close. Without a pipeline, deals fall through the cracks and money walks out the door. A CRM (Customer Relationship Management tool) like Podio, REsimpli, or even a Google Sheet can manage your workflow in the early stages. Tag every lead by status: new inquiry, appointment set, offer made, under contract, buyer assigned, and closed. For a deeper look at organizing your deal flow, read our guide on [Deal Pipeline Management for Real Estate Investors](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/deal-pipeline-management).

Pro Tip: Write down every repeatable task in your business as a simple checklist. What steps do you take from the moment a seller calls to the moment you close? Documenting these processes now makes it ten times easier to hire and train help later. See our guide on [Building SOPs for Your Real Estate Business](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/sops-real-estate-business) for a template you can copy.
Step 7: Plan Your Exit Strategies for Every Deal

A complete wholesaling business plan accounts for what happens when a deal doesn't sell fast. Have a backup plan ready. Can you double-close and list it with an agent? Can you novation the contract and split the upside with the seller? Could you hold it as a rental if the numbers work? Having multiple exits protects your earnest money deposits and your reputation. For a full breakdown of how to decide when to flip, hold, or use a 1031 exchange, read [Exit Strategies: When to Hold, Sell, or 1031](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/real-estate-investor-exit-strategies). The best wholesalers think like investors — not just middlemen.
Step 8: Track Metrics, Refine, and Scale

After your first few deals, sit down with your numbers. What is your cost per lead? Cost per deal? Average assignment fee? Conversion rate from appointment to signed contract? Tracking these weekly tells you where to invest more and where to cut. If direct mail costs you $3,000 per closed deal and cold calling costs you $800, you shift your budget. Scaling from solo operator to a small team means hiring a disposition manager, a lead manager, and eventually a virtual assistant for data work. The jump from $100,000 to $500,000 per year almost always requires delegation. For a full roadmap on growing beyond the solo stage, revisit the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide to see how the foundation connects to long-term wealth building.
